newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sexist advertising thing of the past -- industry.
newsitem.headline: Sexist advertising thing of the past -- industry.

text.p: Times have changed since the 1950s when an advertiser could get away with a picture of a woman next to a car headed by the caption: "Get your husband to buy you one when you pass your test."

Nowadays, with women making more than 70 percent of all purchases -- including cars, life insurance and office equipment -- and with more than half of all advertisements aimed at a female audience, the advertising industry would be crazy to alienate them, Henry d'Anethan of the World Federation of Advertisers said.
"Responsible advertisers have no wish and no need to discriminate against women or offend at least half their audiences," d'Anethan told a European Parliament hearing on women in advertising.

The 1950s advertisement, displayed by Matti Anderson, the director general of the British Advertising Standards Authority, provoked huffs of disbelief from the members of the parliament's committee on women's affairs who organised the hearing to look at ways to prevent offensive and degrading portrayals of women.

German Christian Democrat Marlene Lenz, the author of a parliamentary report on offensive stereotypes of women in advertising, said there was still a need to stamp out advertisements "which simply reconfirm our existing prejudices."

Studies of advertising trends over the last 20 years showed that after a period of men in the kitchen and women at work, the industry was now reverting to images "that suggest women are far better for more menial and bedroom pursuits than for a serious career," Lenz said.
She said she agreed with industry that advertisers should be allowed to self-regulate but she insisted national and European Union anti-discrimination laws needed toughening up.

Degrading stereotypes of women -- and men -- did offend the public but most complaints to the industry regulators were about other matters, Oliver Gray, the director general of the European Adverting Standards Alliance, told the hearing.

Less than 5 percent of all complaints about advertisements between 1992 and 1995 were about the portrayal of the sexes, Gray said, citing a study of the 14 European Union countries that belonged to the Alliance in 1995 (Finland joined in 1996).
He said it would be difficult to set advertising standards to cover the whole EU bloc because sensitivities about taste and decency changed from one country to the next.

A poster for the Hollywood film "The People vs Larry Flynt" showing porn king Flynt crucified on a woman's crotch, caused howls of outrage in France and Germany but barely a murmur in other parts of Europe, ASA head Alderson said.
